revision_note_r5: Revised after plan_judge REJECT of plan@2c8bf8cc173d69d2a34d31efb90e0f21bc27dfe7. Every change is substantive; no qualifier was moved. (1) P-A0 had no declared boundary, so its manifest could not satisfy the Definition of Done. Fixed at the root: **T00 is now a real task** — declared in factory/.planning/decompose.json with a 14-path boundary, with factory/tasks/T00.md written, and T01..T05 now depend on it. The slice is renamed P-T00, its manifest is exactly T00's boundary, and the manifest now also carries factory/tasks/T05.md (omitted from the r4 claim), factory/BLUEPRINT.md, factory/.planning/plan.json, factory/HANDOFF.md and scripts/lib/check_amendments.py — the last three being the files the r4 rebuttal required but did not list. Its verification is no longer greps for isolated words: scripts/lib/check_amendments.py checks that each amended document carries its SUPERSEDED (C-N) marker, that the superseded text is inside a blockquote (no unquoted line may contain a stale token), and that a canonical sentence per conflict appears verbatim in every document that must agree, including plan.json and HANDOFF.md. (2) The --health exception is withdrawn, not reworded. The judge is right that neither an unavailable task goal nor a CI convention can create an exception to CONTRACT 0.2, and the CI premise is additionally false: .github/workflows/factory.yml and scripts/ were checked and neither invokes the CLI at all. 0.2 lists 'a missing argument' among the argv shapes that MUST be rejected, and `pomo --health` supplies no duration. So `pomo --health` is now a rejection, T02's positional goes back to being required (the nargs='?' complication and its silent-default trap disappear with it), and the documents that promised otherwise are amended by new conflict C-6. If the health check is wanted, that is a CONTRACT 0.2 amendment by the exam board before signature — recorded as an open item, not granted here. (3) P-T04's wrong final state for opposite signals pending together is fixed rather than declared residual. The transition record is no longer written by a Python handler in CPython's ascending-signal-number scan order: signal.set_wakeup_fd on an os.pipe() has CPython's C-level handler write the signal number at delivery, so the byte stream is in delivery order, and the render loop waits in select() on that pipe instead of sleeping. A resume delivered before a pause is now applied resume-then-pause and the interval ends paused. What survives is a few-instruction window inside trip_signal, stated honestly and no longer at a timescale any sender can observe. The handler now does nothing at all, so r4's under-warranted 'read the clock inside the handler' argument is gone with it. (4) P-T05 is redesigned, not rescoped. r4's short-write remainder loop broke 0.5's 'one append of the complete record' by construction; there is now exactly one os.write ever, and a short return is rolled back with ftruncate to the pre-write size so no torn line survives the call. Both preconditions the judge rejected are withdrawn: no local-filesystem scoping (the rollback covers a short return anywhere) and no conforming-pre-existing-log precondition (this program is the only writer the contract defines, so 'every line has four fields' is a property of what it writes). Directory durability is no longer an ambiguous singular parent: on the creating run every directory that gained an entry is fsynced — $HOME for .pomo/ and ~/.pomo for log.tsv. (5) P-T03's claim is scoped to the running state, since T04 stores a remaining duration while paused, and its verification now exercises SIGSTOP against a real process in tests/test_clock.py rather than leaving AC-5's stall half to a fake clock. (6) P-T02's verify now runs T01's tests/test_health.py, the regression it owns. (7) I-5 is new: visible/test_pause.py ends in assertWellFormed, so that module cannot pass before T05 lands; the verify commands say so instead of naming a gate that cannot go green.

disputed_review_notes.note: plan_judge r4 (P-T04): 'The admitted wrong final state when opposite signals are pending together is a contract failure, not an acceptable residual: 0.6 contains no spacing exception.'
disputed_review_notes.response: Accepted, and fixed rather than argued. Delivery order is recoverable — just not from the Python-level handlers, which CPython invokes in ascending signal-number order. signal.set_wakeup_fd(w) makes CPython's C-level handler write the signal number to a pipe at delivery, so the bytes are in delivery order; the loop waits in select() on the read end and applies each drained byte in the order it appears. Resume-then-pause now ends paused. One residual is left and it is smaller by orders of magnitude: the order inverts only if the second signal's delivery preempts the first inside the handful of instructions of trip_signal before its write. That is not a spacing exception at any timescale a sender can produce deliberately — it requires the two deliveries to overlap inside one C function — and it is a property of POSIX signal delivery rather than of an interval this implementation picked. It is stated, not claimed away.

disputed_review_notes.note: plan_judge r4 (P-T04): 'The accumulator rebuttal is also overstated — three SIGUSR1 deliveries do not establish duplicate resume application, and both representations already require the same state-change guard.'
disputed_review_notes.response: Accepted in full; the blast-radius rebuttal is deleted. Three pause signals say nothing about duplicate resume application, and the guard is common to both forms. What replaces it is the one difference that is structural rather than statistical: under `deadline = monotonic() + remaining` the pause *destroys* the deadline, so there is no state in which an interval keeps counting against a deadline set before it was paused. Under `deadline += now - paused_at` the old deadline survives the pause and correctness depends on an addition being performed later. AC-6's 'paused time is not deducted' is therefore unrepresentable in the first form and merely absent in the second. That is ADR-2's own argument, and it is adopted verbatim.

disputed_review_notes.note: plan_judge r4 (P-T05): 'Section 0.5 unconditionally requires one complete append and no crash-truncated line; the plan expressly disclaims both after a short write and then performs multiple writes.'
disputed_review_notes.response: Accepted in full. The remainder loop is removed. There is exactly one os.write() of the complete record on every path; a short return is rolled back with os.ftruncate() to the size captured before the write, and the program then reports the failure on stderr and exits non-zero without announcing a completion. So no path leaves a partial record and no path performs a second write. The only case in which the rollback is withheld is a short write that raced a second appender (the pre-write size no longer matches), because truncating there would destroy another process's record; that case is reported, not silently accepted, and its precondition is a full disk plus a concurrent pomo in the same instant.

disputed_review_notes.note: plan_judge r4 (P-T05): 'The local-filesystem and conforming-preexisting-log preconditions are also absent from the contract and therefore weaken it.'
disputed_review_notes.response: Accepted; both are withdrawn from the claim. The local-filesystem scoping was load-bearing only for the short-write case, which the rollback now handles on any filesystem. The conforming-log precondition was unnecessary: under this contract the program is the only writer of ~/.pomo/log.tsv (NG-4, NG-6, NG-7; B-02 is a reader), so 'every line has the same field count and the file ends with a newline' is a property of the records this program writes, and it writes exactly one shape. The operational rule that history is never read or repaired stays in the warrant, where it belongs, as a consequence of AC-8's scale budget.

disputed_review_notes.note: plan_judge r4 (P-T01/P-T02): '--health has no authority in the supplied contract and contradicts 0.2's valid-iff rule ... the plan cannot create an exception to 0.2 from an unavailable task goal or CI convention.'
disputed_review_notes.response: Accepted without reservation, and the check was run: `.github/workflows/factory.yml` and everything under `scripts/` were searched for an invocation of the CLI, and there is none — the workflow's build job runs `pip install -e . || true` and `bash -n`, nothing more. CONTRACT 0.2 lists 'a missing argument' among the shapes that MUST be rejected and `pomo --health` supplies no duration, so it is a rejection. C-6 amends T01.md, BLUEPRINT.md and (already applied) decompose.json's T01 goal; tests/test_health.py keeps its name and asserts the rejection plus entry-point resolution. Restoring the health check would require amending CONTRACT 0.2 before signature, which is the exam board's to do and is recorded as an open item under C-6.

Where an ADR, a task file, a blueprint line or a boundary disagrees with the contract, this plan follows the contract and the disagreement is fixed in the document that is wrong, before a builder reads it. contract_conflicts.contract: 0.4 — the countdown updates 'at least once per second of wall-clock time'; 0.3 — POMO_SECONDS_PER_MINUTE may be any positive decimal.
contract_conflicts.conflict: ADR-1 and factory/tasks/T03.md say the render loop sleeps to the next second boundary, `remaining % 1`. But `remaining` is in *nominal* units, and 0.3 places no bound on the scale factor at either end. Above 60 seconds-per-minute one nominal second is longer than one real second, so the loop refreshes less often than once per wall-clock second and violates 0.4/AC-3 while keeping perfect time. At an exact nominal boundary the remainder is zero, so the loop sleeps zero and can do so repeatedly. And at the held-out suite's smallest scale (0.005, used by `pomo 600`) a nominal second is 83 microseconds, so boundary-sleeping is a CPU-bound frame storm.
contract_conflicts.resolution: Amend ADR-1's render rule and T03.md's 'What to build' bullet to, all in real seconds: step_real = SECONDS_PER_MINUTE / 60; rem = remaining_real % step_real; tick = step_real if rem <= EPS else rem; sleep_for = max(min(tick, 1.0, remaining_real), MIN_SLEEP). ADR-1's decision — the deadline is monotonic and `remaining` is always derived, never decremented — is untouched and adopted verbatim; ADR-1 already states the sleep is a display concern with no effect on when the interval ends.

contract_requirements_no_task_owns.contract: 0.7 — non-zero exit on interrupt before completion; AC-12 — an interrupted interval appends no line.
contract_requirements_no_task_owns.gap: Under ADR-2 this was carried by the `q` abandon path. C-2 removes `q`, so no slice owned it any more. There is no other 'abandon' concept in the contract: 0.6's two signals are the only ones the program handles deliberately. heldout/test_crash.py checks it for SIGKILL, SIGINT and SIGTERM alike.
contract_requirements_no_task_owns.assigned: P-T05, which owns AC-12. The rule is: do not replace the disposition of SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP or SIGQUIT. Stated precisely, because the two halves differ. SIGTERM/SIGHUP/SIGQUIT have no Python handler, so the OS default terminates the process with a non-zero wait status. SIGINT does have one — CPython installs default_int_handler at startup — and it raises KeyboardInterrupt, which left uncaught exits 1 with a traceback on stderr. Both are non-zero, and neither appends anything, because the write sits after the interval reaches zero and not in a finally. The deliberate non-action is therefore: no signal.signal() call for these four, and no `except KeyboardInterrupt` that exits 0. A friendly abandon message is backlog B-04 and must keep the non-zero exit.

integration_notes.note: T03, T04 and T05 each rewrite part of session.py in sequence, and a slice's `verify` runs only the visible modules that can pass at that point plus the unit test its own boundary adds. Ownership: the builder runs its slice's verify; the **inspector** owns the Definition of Done — `bash factory/tests/run-visible.sh` twice in a row plus `run-heldout.sh` — and that gate cannot be delegated to a builder, because no builder worktree contains factory/tests/heldout/. This is why the DoD asks for the full suite rather than an aggregate of the five verify commands.

T02 sits outside the T01→T03→T04→T05 spine and touches only cli.py, so it can land at any point after T00 and T01. Its boundary is disjoint from every other build task, so there is no merge hazard — but it is the only slice whose verify exercises the reject path, and after C-6 it is also the slice that can regress T01's argv behaviour without owning it. That is why P-T02's verify runs tests/test_health.py. Later slices must not move validation out of cli.py to reach it.

C-2 deletes the `q` abandon path that T04.md and ADR-2 describe. T05.md's 'not on T04's q path' instruction becomes vacuous — the equivalent rule is 'the write is not in a finally and not reachable from any signal path'. R-3 carries the exit-code half, and states the SIGINT case precisely because CPython does not leave SIGINT at its OS default.

T00 is a prerequisite of all five build tasks, including T01 — C-6 amends T01.md and BLUEPRINT.md, so T01 is no longer independent of the amendments. The ordering is not bureaucratic: T03.md, T04.md and T05.md each open with 'read factory/adr/ADR-N.md before writing code', so an unamended ADR is the first thing the builder reads and plan.json is the second, if at all. T00 changes no file under src/, tests/ or factory/tests/, so it cannot move either suite; its only failure mode is leaving two documents disagreeing, which is exactly what its verify checks.

The visible suite is not fully green until T05 lands, and no slice's verify pretends otherwise. visible/test_log.py needs T05 by definition. Less obviously, visible/test_pause.py's AC-6 test ends with `self.assertWellFormed(self.read_log_bytes(), expect_lines=1)` — so the pause module cannot pass at T04, whose boundary contains no log writer. P-T04 therefore verifies against test_run plus its own tests/test_pause.py, and P-T05's verify is the first gate that runs `run-visible.sh test_pause`. HANDOFF.md's 'run the whole suite before you finish' is corrected to match: modules owned by tasks that have not landed yet will fail, and that is not your slice's failure — every criterion an earlier slice established still is.

T04 changes how the render loop waits, not how long. T03 pins the duration (the C-4 formula); T04 replaces `time.sleep(sleep_for)` with `select.select([wakeup_r], [], [], sleep_for)` so that a signal wakes the loop immediately instead of at the end of the current sleep. The formula, the units, and the deadline are T03's and stay untouched — a T04 that reintroduces its own polling interval is re-solving a problem select() already solved and reintroduces the accounting error I-1's ordering exists to avoid.

slices.warrant: time.monotonic() counts real elapsed time across a SIGSTOP — unlike time.process_time(), which does not — and cannot be stepped by NTP or DST — unlike time.time(), which can. The failure AC-5 hunts is a program that infers elapsed time from its own sleeps, which under-reports by exactly the stall; deriving `remaining` on every read makes that failure unrepresentable rather than merely absent, which is a stronger property than making it absent. The claim is scoped to the running state on purpose: T04 stores exactly one duration, at a pause, and a paused interval has no deadline to derive from — the pause destroys it. Two units exist in this program and conflating them is the likeliest way to fail, so they are named here rather than left to the reader. `time.monotonic()` returns **real** seconds, so `deadline - monotonic()` is `remaining_real`. The display, the CLI argument, and the log are in **nominal** seconds. The conversion is `remaining_nominal = remaining_real * 60 / SECONDS_PER_MINUTE`, one multiplication applied to a freshly-derived absolute value on each read — so it accumulates nothing, in the same way and for the same reason that `remaining_real` itself accumulates nothing. Only the deadline is computed from a conversion, once: `deadline = monotonic() + minutes * SECONDS_PER_MINUTE`. ADR-1's subordinate render rule is amended here (C-4) and the amendment is load-bearing at both ends of 0.3's unbounded range. Above 60 seconds-per-minute one nominal second exceeds one real second, so `remaining % 1` on nominal units drops the display below 0.4's wall-clock floor. Below it the boundary rule degenerates: the held-out suite runs `pomo 600` at scale 0.005, where a nominal second is 83 microseconds, so sleeping to each nominal boundary means tens of thousands of frames and a CPU-bound loop. And at an exact boundary the remainder is *zero*, so a naive `sleep(remaining_real % step_real)` sleeps zero, wakes at the same boundary, and can sleep zero again — a spin the formula must exclude by construction rather than by luck. The rule is therefore, all in real seconds: `step_real = SECONDS_PER_MINUTE / 60`; `rem = remaining_real % step_real`; `tick = step_real if rem <= EPS else rem` (EPS a small real epsilon — at a boundary the next boundary is a full step away); `sleep_for = max(min(tick, 1.0, remaining_real), MIN_SLEEP)` with MIN_SLEEP about 5ms. The upper bound of 1.0 is 0.4's wall-clock floor; `remaining_real` stops the loop overshooting the deadline; MIN_SLEEP guarantees the clock advances between iterations, which is what makes 'the loop cannot spin' a property of the formula rather than a hope about floating-point remainders. MIN_SLEEP costs nothing that matters: it can delay the end of an interval by at most 5ms against a 1s tolerance, and it bounds the frame rate at 200/s where the unbounded rule would emit 12,000/s. Sleeping to a boundary rather than a flat interval is still right, for ADR-1's stated reason: each sleep overshoots slightly, so a flat interval lets the tick phase creep, whereas re-deriving the distance to the next boundary from the clock resets the phase every tick. This is a display change only and cannot affect the end time — ADR-1 already establishes that the sleep's duration, jitter and repetition count have no bearing on the deadline. SIGUSR1/2 need no daemon, open no endpoint, and are not SIGSTOP, so AC-13 and NG-7 still hold trivially and AC-5's 'a stall is not a pause' stays clearly distinct. ADR-2's time accounting is adopted unchanged and is still what carries AC-6 and AC-7: pause captures `remaining` once, as a *duration*, and resume sets `deadline = monotonic() + remaining`. The property that matters is structural, not statistical — a pause **destroys** the deadline, so there is no state in which an interval keeps counting against a deadline set before it was paused, and AC-6's 'paused time is not deducted' is unrepresentable rather than merely absent. Under `deadline += now - paused_at` the old deadline survives the pause and correctness depends on an addition being performed later; that is the whole of the objection, and the r4 blast-radius argument that went beyond it is withdrawn. What changes with the mechanism is how the loop waits and how transitions are ordered, and this is where revision 5 differs from revision 4 substantively rather than in wording. Revision 4 recorded transitions from Python-level signal handlers and then admitted that two opposite signals pending at one check point are applied in CPython's ascending signal-number order, not delivery order — so a resume delivered before a pause ended running when the user meant paused. That is a 0.6 violation, 0.6 has no spacing exception, and it is fixable: delivery order *is* recoverable, just not from the Python-level handlers. `signal.set_wakeup_fd(w)` makes CPython's C-level handler write the signal number to a pipe **at delivery**, before any Python code runs. So the design is: `r, w = os.pipe()`; the write end is set non-blocking and passed to set_wakeup_fd; Python handlers are installed for SIGUSR1 and SIGUSR2 that do nothing at all — installing them is what replaces the default terminating disposition and what causes CPython's C handler, and therefore the wakeup write, to run. The render loop then waits in `select.select([r], [], [], sleep_for)` instead of `time.sleep(sleep_for)`, and on wake drains the pipe with one os.read, takes one clock.monotonic() reading, and applies each byte's transition in the order the bytes appear, ignoring any byte that is not SIGUSR1 or SIGUSR2. Three things follow. Ordering: the byte sequence is delivery order, so resume-then-pause is applied resume-then-pause and the interval ends paused — the failure the judge refused is gone rather than tolerated. Latency: the loop is woken *by the delivery*, so the timestamp it takes is behind delivery by the interpreter's wake path, not by an interval this implementation picked; PEP 475 restarts the interrupted select with a recomputed timeout, and the byte is already in the pipe, so the restarted call returns at once. Safety: the handler does nothing, so the async-signal-safety question disappears entirely along with revision 4's argument about reading a clock inside a handler. One residual survives and it is stated as a fact about POSIX signal delivery, not as a tolerance: if a second signal is delivered while the first signal's C handler is between entry and its write, the two bytes land inverted. That is a window of a few instructions inside one C function — not a spacing requirement any sender can meet or miss deliberately, and both suites space their signals 0.3s or more apart in any case. Two further properties of signals are designed around rather than assumed away. Non-realtime signals do not queue: three SIGUSR1s delivered in quick succession may produce one delivery and one byte. That is harmless *here*, and only because 0.6 mandates idempotence — a coalesced repeat is semantically identical to the single signal it collapses into, which is exactly what heldout/test_pause_semantics.py's three-SIGUSR1 case checks. And idempotence itself is implemented as a state-machine guard, not a counter: a drained SIGUSR1 while already paused, or SIGUSR2 while already running, is discarded with its timestamp, so neither re-captures `remaining` from a clock that is not running. Pending transitions are drained and applied **before** expiry is evaluated, which closes the race where a pause lands between the deadline being reached and the completion path running. While paused the frame content is frozen and the clock is not consulted — there is no deadline to consult — but the frozen frame is re-emitted under the same 1.0s upper bound, so 0.4's cadence holds under either reading of 'while an interval runs'. AC-13 is unaffected: an os.pipe() is neither a process nor a socket, nothing inherits it because nothing is spawned, and both ends close when the process exits; heldout/test_no_daemon.py's listening-socket check has nothing to find.
rebuttal: ADR-2 is upheld over the contract and `p`/`q`-on-stdin is built. test_pause.py fails at the first signal (default SIGUSR1 disposition terminates the process), and the keypress path is unreachable anyway under stdin=DEVNULL. This is the single most likely way this slice fails, because the task file and the ADR both instruct it until C-2 lands.

The wakeup pipe is skipped and transitions are recorded from the Python handlers instead. Everything passes — both suites space their signals 0.3s apart — while opposite signals delivered inside one check point are applied in ascending signal-number order, so a resume-then-pause pair leaves the interval running. That is the 0.6 violation revision 5 exists to remove, and no test in either suite will report it.

set_wakeup_fd is used but no Python handler is installed for SIGUSR1/SIGUSR2. CPython only writes the wakeup byte from the C handler it installs via signal.signal(), and without it the default disposition still terminates the process — the pause path is dead and the symptom is the same as having done nothing.

The write end of the pipe is left blocking. CPython requires the wakeup fd to be non-blocking and reports an error on the write path instead of delivering the byte, so signals are silently lost under load.

The loop keeps `time.sleep(sleep_for)` and merely reads the pipe afterwards. The wake is then bounded by the render interval again: every pause and every resume charges up to one interval of running time as paused time, twice per cycle, against AC-7's 1s budget over ten cycles.

T04 introduces its own short polling step (say 50ms) 'to be responsive', undoing I-6. That is the accounting error above in a smaller form, and it passes locally on an idle machine and degrades on a loaded one — a flake that reruns green.

Pause stores a timestamp (`paused_at`) and resume computes `deadline = old_deadline + (now - paused_at)`. Applied exactly once and in order, that is algebraically exact; the objection is that the old deadline survives the pause, so an interval can keep counting against a deadline set before it was paused if the addition is missed. Storing a duration destroys the deadline and removes the state that failure needs.

Bytes drained from the pipe are sorted, de-duplicated, or reduced to a set 'to handle coalescing'. Delivery order is exactly what the pipe was introduced to preserve, and sorting throws it away — reintroducing the ascending-order bug through the back door.

Bytes that are not SIGUSR1 or SIGUSR2 are treated as transitions. Any signal with a Python handler writes to the same pipe — SIGINT has one by default — so an unfiltered drain turns a Ctrl-C into a pause.

Either signal is treated as a toggle. One SIGUSR1 pauses and the next resumes, which passes the single-cycle visible test and fails heldout/test_pause_semantics.py's idempotency case, where three SIGUSR1s must leave the interval paused.

Repeated identical signals are counted rather than applied as idempotent state transitions. Non-realtime signals coalesce, so the count depends on scheduler timing and the answer changes between runs.

Pending transitions are drained after expiry is evaluated rather than before. A pause delivered in the window between the deadline passing and the completion path running is applied to an interval that has already ended, so the completion path runs against a paused clock: ran_seconds is wrong, or the process never exits.

SIGUSR1 while already paused re-captures `remaining` from a clock that is not running, driving the stored duration toward zero or negative; SIGUSR2 while running re-derives a deadline from a stale duration and restarts the interval. Both break 0.6's idempotence requirement.

The display stops entirely while paused. 0.4 requires an update at least once per wall-clock second while an interval runs, and 'paused' is not obviously outside that; re-emitting the frozen frame costs nothing and removes the argument.

P-T04's verify is written as `run-visible.sh test_pause`, which cannot pass at T04 — that module's AC-6 test ends with assertWellFormed on a log no slice has written yet (I-5). The builder reads a red suite as its own failure and starts changing pause code that is correct.

slices.claim: Completing an interval appends exactly one four-field TSV record — ended_at, planned_minutes, started_at, ran_seconds — to $HOME/.pomo/log.tsv, resolved from os.environ at write time, built whole in memory and handed to the kernel by exactly one os.write() on a descriptor opened O_WRONLY|O_APPEND|O_CREAT, fsynced — together with every directory that gained an entry on the run that creates the path — before the completion summary is printed. No pre-existing byte is changed; ~/.pomo/ and log.tsv are created on the completion path only; every line in the file has the same four non-empty tab-free fields and the file ends with a newline; and an interval interrupted or killed before completion appends nothing and exits non-zero. There is no second write on any path: if the single write returns short, the partial bytes are removed with os.ftruncate() back to the size captured before the write and the program reports the failure on stderr and exits non-zero without announcing a completion, so no code path leaves a record ending mid-line. The one case in which the rollback is withheld is a short write that raced another appender — the file is no longer the size the rollback assumes, and truncating would destroy that other process's record — and that case is reported rather than repaired; its precondition is a full disk and a second pomo appending in the same instant.

slices.warrant: The column order changes from ADR-3's. CONTRACT 0.5 pins field 1 to the interval completion time (parsed with datetime.fromisoformat) and field 2 to the duration in whole minutes equal to the CLI argument; visible/test_log.py asserts `line.split('\t')[1] == '1'` and heldout/test_arg_boundaries.py asserts the same field equals '600'. ADR-3's order puts the completion time in field 2 and the minutes in field 3, so it fails on a one-character index. Reordering to (ended_at, planned_minutes, started_at, ran_seconds) keeps all four columns and the fixed count of 4, and leaves ADR-3's actual argument for AC-10 intact: every field is still generated from an integer or a timestamp, so no field can contain a tab or a newline, and AC-10's per-record half is satisfied by the column choice rather than by escaping logic that could be got wrong. Atomicity is where revision 4 was wrong, and revision 5 changes the mechanism rather than the wording of the claim. 0.5 does not merely assert a property, it prescribes the mechanism and then draws the conclusion: 'The line is written as one append of the complete record plus its newline, and is flushed to the OS before the completion summary is printed. A crash therefore never leaves a truncated line.' Revision 4's short-write remainder loop broke the premise of that sentence — after a short write and a follow-up write there is no longer one append — and then disclaimed the conclusion. So the remainder loop is gone. There is exactly one os.write() of the complete record on every path. If it returns short, the bytes it did write are already on disk and raising cannot unwrite them, so the program removes them: os.fstat(fd).st_size is captured *before* the write, and a short return of n bytes is rolled back with os.ftruncate(fd, size_before) — but only after re-checking that the file is exactly size_before + n, because if another appender landed in between, truncating would destroy that process's record. Either way the program then writes the failure to stderr, exits non-zero, and does not print a completion summary; it never claims an interval was recorded that was not. What that buys is the unconditional form of the claim: no filesystem precondition is needed for the short-write case, because the rollback works wherever a short return can happen, including NFS and FUSE where revision 4 had to scope the claim away. What remains is the case 0.5 actually legislates — a completed single write that is then interrupted by a fatal signal — and there the mechanism is the contract's own: a ~60-byte write to a regular file copies into the page cache without an interruptible sleep, and a pending SIGKILL is acted on at a syscall boundary, so the record is in the file or it is not. Nothing here claims atomicity against power loss or media failure, which no userspace append provides and which 0.5's flush-before-announce clause is the contract's chosen answer to. The exposure is real and not hypothetical, which is why the mechanism has to be exact: heldout/test_crash.py sweeps SIGKILL across 2.00-2.30s of a 2.0s interval against a 200,000-record log, deliberately aimed at the completion-write window, so 'the write only happens at the end' narrows the target to sub-millisecond but does not remove it. What O_APPEND itself provides is narrower than its reputation: seek-to-end and write are one indivisible step *with respect to other writers*, so the record lands at the true end of file and concurrent appenders interleave whole records. It says nothing about crashes, and this warrant does not lean on it for that. AC-10's whole-file half needs no precondition either, and revision 4's conforming-log precondition is withdrawn: under this contract nothing else writes ~/.pomo/log.tsv — NG-6 forbids a database, NG-4 forbids sync, NG-7 forbids a daemon, and the only reader contemplated is backlog B-02 — so 'every line has the same field count and the file ends with a newline' is a property of the records this program writes, and it writes exactly one shape, whole or not at all. The related operational rule stands on its own footing: the history is never read and never repaired, because heldout/test_log_scale.py's budget of interval+2s against a 50,000-record log forbids per-record work proportional to the file, and because silently 'completing' a line that something else truncated makes damage permanent instead of visible. Its harnesses are consistent with this by construction — visible/test_log.py builds history by really running intervals, and test_log_scale.py probes the implementation's own field count with field_count() and passes it to seed_log(fields=...) — but the claim does not depend on that. Durability needs more than the file fsync. os.fsync(fd) makes the record's bytes durable, but a newly created pathname is a directory entry, and an entry is not durable until the directory that holds it is synced. On the run that creates the path, two directories can gain an entry: $HOME gains `.pomo` and ~/.pomo gains `log.tsv`. So existence is checked before creating anything, and each directory that was in fact created — or that the log file was created in — is opened O_RDONLY and fsynced. That is O(1), happens only on the creating run, and costs nothing against the scale budget. os.makedirs(exist_ok=True) plus O_CREAT run only on the completion path, so AC-9 holds without ~/.pomo appearing as a side effect of an interval the user abandoned. The write call sits after the interval reaches zero — not in a finally, not on the exception path, not reachable from any signal handler — so AC-12 holds because control never reaches it, not because a flag says so. Ordering is pinned by 0.5 and checked by heldout/test_crash.py's third case: the fsync precedes the AC-4 completion summary, so the user is never told an interval finished that is not durable. 0.7's other half is carried by not replacing the disposition of SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP or SIGQUIT — with the precision R-3 states, since CPython's default_int_handler means SIGINT raises KeyboardInterrupt rather than dying at the OS default, and the observable result is still a non-zero exit with nothing appended. Three detail rules, each because 0.3 or 0.5 says so and no task file repeats it: the path is computed from os.environ inside the write function at run time, not cached at import; planned_minutes is the CLI argument verbatim; and ran_seconds is counted in nominal seconds, so the same completed interval writes the same record at every POMO_SECONDS_PER_MINUTE. Timestamps come from time.time() in UTC at second precision with a `Z` suffix — datetime.fromisoformat accepts `Z` from Python 3.11 onward, and this repo runs 3.11.4 — and never from T03's monotonic clock, which has no epoch and no cross-process meaning.
rebuttal: ADR-3's column order is used verbatim, because both the ADR and T05.md present it as a fixed table and call it 'fixed forever'. test_log.py's field-2 assertion then fails, while assertWellFormed still accepts field 1 because started_at also parses as ISO — so the failure surfaces as one confusing assertion rather than as an obvious ordering mistake.

os.write()'s return value is not checked at all. A short write leaves a truncated line on disk and the program prints a completion summary — the exact AC-10/AC-11 failure the design exists to prevent, arrived at through the one line that looks like boilerplate.

The return value is checked and a short write raises. The bytes are already on disk, so raising reports failure while leaving the truncated line in place — strictly worse than not checking, because it looks like careful error handling.

Revision 4's remainder loop is written instead of the rollback. There are then two instants at which a partial record is on disk, 0.5's 'one append of the complete record' is false by construction, and heldout/test_crash.py aims its kills at exactly that window.

The rollback truncates without re-checking the file size. If another appender landed between our short write and the ftruncate, its record is destroyed — turning a rare local failure into data loss for a different process, which is worse than the torn line it was fixing.

The pre-write size is taken with lseek on an O_APPEND descriptor rather than os.fstat, or is taken after the write. Either way the rollback truncates to the wrong offset and can cut into records that were already durable.
The trailing newline is written in a second os.write() in the normal path. The single-write property is gone, and with it the only argument that carries AC-11.

open(path, 'a') or any buffered writer is used instead of os.open + os.write. On SIGKILL the user-space buffer is discarded outright, so a completed interval the user was told had finished is simply absent (AC-8). Truncation is also possible but needs the record to straddle a buffer boundary, so the common symptom is silent loss, not a torn line, and it is invisible to any test that does not kill the process.

The file is fsynced but the directories are not, on the run that creates ~/.pomo/log.tsv. The record's bytes are durable and the entries naming them are not, so a power loss just after the first-ever completion can leave the file unreachable — the durability gap that survives a correct-looking fsync.
Only one directory is synced when both were created. Syncing ~/.pomo makes log.tsv's entry durable while .pomo's own entry in $HOME is not, which is the same gap one level up.

The pre-existing log is inspected to decide whether to prepend a newline, or is read to verify its field count. Either reads history that an append must not depend on — heldout/test_log_scale.py's 50,000-record budget is written to catch per-record work proportional to the file — and 'completing' a previously truncated line makes damage permanent instead of visible.

ran_seconds is recorded in real seconds rather than nominal ones. POMO_SECONDS_PER_MINUTE then changes a logged value, which 0.3 explicitly forbids, and heldout/test_log_scale.py is named for exactly this comparison.

The log path is resolved once at import via os.path.expanduser or a module constant. Both harnesses set HOME per spawned process and examlib.fresh_home() changes it mid-test, so this works for the first case and then writes to the wrong place — possibly the developer's real ~/.pomo.
The write is placed in a finally, or wrapped around the whole run. Every exception path and SIGINT then appends a line and AC-12 fails.

A KeyboardInterrupt handler is added to print a tidy message and it exits 0, or a SIGTERM handler is installed that returns without exiting. 0.7's non-zero-on-interrupt is then violated by code written to improve the user experience, and heldout/test_crash.py checks SIGINT and SIGTERM as well as SIGKILL.

fsync runs after the summary is printed rather than before it, so a crash in that window tells the user an interval completed that never reached disk — a 0.5 violation the visible suite does not detect and heldout/test_crash.py does.

ran_seconds formats to an empty string, or the record is built with a trailing tab, for a very short scaled interval; assertWellFormed rejects any empty field, so a formatting choice fails a criterion that has nothing to do with the log's purpose.

A lock file or a temp-file-plus-rename is added to 'protect' the write. Rename risks the whole history to protect one record and rewrites bytes AC-8 requires untouched; a lock file adds a stale-lock failure mode, guards a threat O_APPEND already handles, and addresses nothing about SIGKILL.
